extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers and experimentalists (educated readers of 17th‑century natural philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and designing experiments and arguments to show whether new substances or principles can be produced (or resolved) by fire or other operations; includes weighing, distillation, apparatus, controls, conceptual clarity, and engagement with prior authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass accounting (weigh before and after)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh components (earth, plant, etc.) before and after experiments to detect material changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple experiments record weights precisely (e.g., 'Weighed the Pompion with the Stalk and Leaves... three pound wanting a quarter' and subsequently weighing the earth after baking). Dry the earth in an oven and re-weigh (repeat drying if necessary) to ensure loss is not due to retained moisture. Note and explain any change in weight (e.g., the gardener 'found the Earth wanted a Pound and a halfe of what it was formerly').

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and choice of inputs to avoid contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose and control input materials (water, soil, seed) to avoid confounding by external seminal principles or airborne impurities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer spring or distilled water to rain-water because rain is 'more discernably a kinde of πανσπερμια' and may contain 'steams of several Bodies wandering in the Air' that could impregnate experiments. Ensure neighbouring earth cannot enter the vessel (use a tinned plate perforated with holes to exclude outside soil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and long-duration trials for robust inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat experiments and, where relevant, run them over long durations to accumulate evidence and observe slow effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helmont's five-year willow experiment and multiple repeated trials are cited as notable: 'Five years being efflux'd, he took out the Tree and weighed it'. The author intends to repeat trials with multiple seeds in the same pot to make results 'more Conspicuous.' Acknowledge that long durations may deter some observers but strengthen conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed record-keeping and reporting of experimental particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve full written accounts of experimental circumstances so results can be evaluated and repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes lost accounts undermine insistence on results: 'I have unhappily lost the particular Account my Gardiner writ me up of the Circumstances, I dare not insist upon them.' Record all conditions (timing, drying cycles, weights, apparatus) to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation and analysis of products
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply distillation and subsequent analysis to identify distinct substances obtained from experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: distilling a spearmint cutting grown in water yielded 'some Phlegme, a little Empyreumaticall Spirit, a small Quantity of adust Oyl, and a Caput mortuum.' Use retorts and distillations to separate components and characterise what the fire yields rather than relying on appearance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate apparatus and control of operational variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proper vessels and control heating/regimes (oven, retort, graduated fire) to ensure experimental integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods described include drying earth 'in an Oven', planting in 'an Earthen pot', using 'a plate of Iron tinn'd over and perforated' to exclude external soil, and employing 'a Graduall Fire in a Retort' or 'the Fire at length very Vehement' when needed. Apparatus and the degree/timing of heating affect outcomes and must be reported and controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and testing of alternative explanations/confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively consider and test alternate causes (dust loss, contamination, pre-existing seminal principles) for observed changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author questions whether weight loss was 'in the Ordering... in Dust (and the like) wasted' and warns that rainwater or imbued seminal particles might explain apparent generation. Design experiments that can distinguish true generation from such confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurement preferred over qualitative impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on measurements (weights, yields) rather than mere appearance or anecdotes to support claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly cites specific weights for pumpkins, cucumbers, branches and earth; these numbers form the basis for inferring transformation of water into plant matter ('164 pound of the Roots, Wood, and Bark ... seem to have Sprung from the Water').

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical evaluation of extraordinary agents and claims (e.g., Alkahest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat claims about universal solvents or miraculous agents with skepticism unless independently verifiable; do not accept arguments reliant solely on such hard-to-reproduce processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helmont's Alkahest and related claims are noted as 'so uneasie to be made and to be judg'd of' and 'cannot be satisfactorily Examin'd by You and Me.' The author therefore prefers evidence from repeatable, inspectable operations over single, extraordinary assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test across classes of materials to assess generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt similar experiments on vegetables, animals, and minerals to see whether observed transformations are general or class-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests trying tobacco, various speedy-growing seeds, and other bodies 'other then Vegetables' to evaluate whether salts, spirits, earth, and oil can be produced from water across different kinds of matter. Examples include attempts to obtain glass from vegetables or water from quicksilver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual clarity: define theoretical terms (e.g., 'mistion')
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear definitions of theoretical concepts and competing hypotheses (e.g., whether mixt bodies are true unities or juxtapositions of corpuscles) because conceptual differences change what experiments are taken to show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts the Peripatetic 'mistion' (mutual penetration so that every minute part contains all four elements) with the older notion of juxta-positioned corpuscles (each retaining its nature). The cloth-thread analogy (white and black threads interwoven producing gray) is given to clarify how a mixture might be conceived. Clear definitions guide both interpretation of experiments and theoretical inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance empirical work with critical engagement with authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use past authors and authorities (Helmont, Boyle, Sennertus, ancient philosophers) as sources of leads, but critically assess their credibility and avoid uncritical acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites Helmont, Helmontian experiments, and ancient authorities (Thales, Plutarch) but warns of 'Extravagancies and Untruths' in Helmont's other writings that make some testimonies suspect. He uses both his own experiments and appeals to other experimenters but notes when independent verification is needed.
